title: Claude Can See My Screen. Here’s What It Gets Wrong.
partialText:
A technical deep-dive into the AI vision layer behind Ezzi — how it reads a coding problem off a screenshot, where it quietly breaks, and which failures I actually engineered around versus the ones I just live with.

TL;DR — Ezzi captures a screenshot of your interview problem and an AI reads it off the pixels. The surprising part is how well that works now. The useful part is where it doesn’t. I’ll walk through the real pipeline (a cheap Sonnet model reads the screen, an expensive Opus model solves from the transcript and never sees the image), the failure modes I hit in production, and an honest split between the ones I fixed and the ones that are still just limitations.

Here’s the Situation

Ezzi is an open-source interview assistant. You hit a shortcut, it captures the coding problem on your screen, an AI reads it, and you get a solution rendered in an overlay that stays invisible to screen sharing.

Vision is the front door to the whole thing. Everything else, the solution, the thought process, the complexity analysis, depends on one assumption: that the model correctly read what was on the screen. If it misreads, it doesn’t fail loudly. It confidently solves the wrong problem and hands you a clean, well-commented answer to a question nobody asked.

I wrote a piece a while back on the OS-level tricks that make the window invisible. This is the other half. Making the window disappear was a hardware-and-compositor problem with mostly deterministic answers. Reading the screen is an AI problem, which means the answers are probabilistic and the failures are subtle. Subtle is worse.

So let me show you what’s actually behind “Claude can see my screen”, and then let me be honest about where it gets things wrong.

What “Claude Can See My Screen” Actually Means

The first thing worth clearing up: there isn’t one model doing this. There are two, and they do very different jobs.

When you capture a problem in Live Interview mode, the screenshot goes to a cheap, deterministic model whose only job is to read the screen and classify what it sees. Here’s that stage:

// src/integrations/prompts/catalog/extract-problem/extract-problem.prompt.ts
private readonly modelParams: ClaudeModelParams = {
  model: 'claude-sonnet-4-6',
  max_tokens: 10_000,
  temperature: 0,
};

Temperature zero is deliberate. This stage isn’t supposed to be creative. It’s supposed to transcribe the problem statement from the image and label it, the same way every time, given the same pixels.

The output of that stage is text. That text, the transcribed problem, is what gets handed to the second model, the one that actually solves:

// src/integrations/prompts/catalog/solve/solve.prompt.ts
private readonly modelParams: ClaudeModelParams = {
  model: 'claude-opus-4-8',
  max_tokens: 20_000,
  effort: 'high',
};

Now here’s the part that matters more than anything else in this article. Look at how the solve stage calls the model:

// src/integrations/prompts/catalog/solve/solve.prompt.ts
const response = await this.claudeService.callModel({
  systemPrompt: SYSTEM_PROMPT,
  userPrompt: promptText,
  images: [], // <- the solver never sees the screenshot
  modelParams: this.modelParams,
  jsonSchema: { /* thoughts, code, complexity, problem_statement */ },
});

images: []. The expensive reasoning model, Opus, never sees your screen. It solves entirely from the transcript that Sonnet produced. The model that reads the pixels and the model that does the thinking are two different models, and the only thing passing between them is a string.

This is a reasonable architecture. Sonnet is cheaper and faster, and reading text off a clean IDE screenshot is not a job that needs the most powerful model available. Splitting it also lets me gate bad screenshots before paying for an expensive solve (more on that shortly).

But it has a consequence that defines the entire failure surface: if the transcription is wrong, nothing downstream can catch it. Opus has no pixels to fall back on. It trusts the string.

Here’s the full shape of it.

The whole thing runs against the Anthropic SDK with a tight budget:

// src/integrations/ai-models/claude/claude.service.ts
this.anthropic = new Anthropic({
  timeout: 60_000,
  maxRetries: 2,
});

Sixty seconds, two retries. An interview doesn’t give you the luxury of a slow answer.

The Capture Layer: What the Model Actually Receives

Before any model sees anything, the desktop app has to grab the screen and turn it into something the API will accept. There’s no fancy capture pipeline here, just the OS doing the work:

// electron/screenshot.helper.ts
private async captureScreenshotMac(): Promise<Buffer> {
  const tmpPath = path.join(app.getPath('temp'), `${uuidv4()}.png`);
  await execFileAsync('screencapture', ['-x', tmpPath]);
  const buffer = await fs.promises.readFile(tmpPath);
  await fs.promises.unlink(tmpPath);
  return buffer;
}

macOS gets screencapture, Windows gets a PowerShell CopyFromScreen call, Linux gets gnome-screenshot. Native PNG, full resolution, straight from the OS.

That PNG is then base64-encoded and sent up. And this is where the first quiet trade-off lives. Claude’s vision API has a size limit, and a full-resolution screenshot of a 4K or multi-monitor setup can blow right past it. So the app compresses, but only when it has to:

// electron/screenshot.helper.ts
private static readonly MAX_IMAGE_SIZE = 3932160; // ~3.75 MB
private static readonly QUALITY_STEPS = [90, 85, 80, 70];
 
private compressIfNeeded(buffer: Buffer): { data: Buffer; ext: string } {
  if (buffer.length <= ScreenshotHelper.MAX_IMAGE_SIZE) {
    return { data: buffer, ext: '.png' }; // small enough, stays lossless
  }
  const image = nativeImage.createFromBuffer(buffer);
  for (const quality of ScreenshotHelper.QUALITY_STEPS) {
    const jpegBuffer = image.toJPEG(quality);
    if (jpegBuffer.length <= ScreenshotHelper.MAX_IMAGE_SIZE) {
      return { data: jpegBuffer, ext: '.jpg' };
    }
  }
  // last resort: ship the most-compressed version even if still over
  const last = ScreenshotHelper.QUALITY_STEPS.at(-1);
  return { data: image.toJPEG(last), ext: '.jpg' };
}

If your screenshot is under the limit, it stays a lossless PNG and the model gets crisp text. If it’s over, it gets walked down a JPEG quality ladder until it fits. JPEG is lossy, and the thing it’s worst at is exactly what we care about: sharp edges on small text. Compression artifacts smear the boundaries between characters, and small monospace code is nothing but sharp edges on small characters.

Here’s the honest part. There is no legibility check anywhere in that function. Nothing measures whether the compressed text is still readable. If you’re on a giant display and the screenshot gets pushed down to quality 70, the model is reading slightly mushy characters, and nobody told it (or you) that the input quality dropped. It just does its best with what it got.

For most people on a normal laptop this never triggers, the PNG is well under 3.75 MB and stays lossless. But it’s a real edge, and pretending it isn’t would be dishonest.

Where the Vision Actually Breaks

Now the part you came for. These are the failure modes I’ve actually seen, sorted by how much I was able to do about them.

1. The split brain: a misread the solver can’t catch

Go back to images: []. Because Opus solves from text and never sees the screen, any character the Sonnet stage gets wrong is baked in permanently.

Vision models misread the things you’d expect a human to squint at. rn rendered in a thin font reads as m. A lowercase l reads as a 1. A capital O reads as a 0. In a problem statement, "the array nums" surviving as "the array nuns" is harmless, the solver figures out the intent. But a misread in a constraint (n <= 10^5 becoming n <= 10^6) or in a sample input quietly changes the problem, and Opus solves the changed version with total confidence.

Temperature zero makes this deterministic, which is a double-edged thing. The same screenshot misreads the same way every time. Stable, but stably wrong. Re-shooting the screenshot (slightly different framing, a cleaner crop) is the only real recovery, because it changes the pixels going into the one stage that looks at pixels.

People sometimes assume the “readable variable names” toggle is the fix here. It isn’t, and I want to be precise about that. Here’s what that toggle actually does:

// src/integrations/prompts/catalog/shared-snippets.ts
export const READABLE_VAR_NAMES_INSTRUCTION =
  '

Use descriptive, human-readable variable names that convey ' +
  'meaning (e.g. `leftIndex` instead of `l`, `currentSum` instead ' +
  'of `s`, `nodeCount` instead of `n`). ...';

That’s an instruction about the code Opus writes, not about the text Sonnet reads. It makes the output easier to explain out loud in an interview. It does nothing to recover a misread on the way in. Two different problems that happen to both involve variable names, and conflating them would be selling you a fix that doesn’t exist.

2. The wrong screenshot entirely (the fix I’m proudest of)

The most common failure in practice isn’t a subtle misread. It’s that you captured the wrong thing. You meant to grab the problem, but the screenshot caught your inbox, a billing page, the login screen, or a Slack window.

If every capture went straight to Opus, every one of those would burn an expensive solve and hand you a “solution” to your inbox. So the cheap Sonnet stage doesn’t just transcribe, it classifies. This is the classification gate, and it’s the piece of this system I’m happiest with.

The prompt forces the screen into one of six buckets:

// src/integrations/prompts/catalog/extract-problem/extract-problem.constants.ts
'- DSA: Data structures & algorithms problem (LeetCode, HackerRank...)
' +
'- SQL: Database query problem (SQL challenges, query writing tasks)
' +
'- SYSTEM_DESIGN: System design question (architecture, scalability...)
' +
'- BEHAVIORAL: Behavioral interview question (non-technical, soft skills)
' +
'- NOT_A_PROBLEM: Screenshot does not contain any programming problem ' +
'  (chat apps, billing pages, login screens, browsers, calendars...)
' +
'- OTHER: Contains a programming task that does not fit the above
'

That classification comes back as a structured field, and the command layer decides whether to proceed:

// src/solutions/app-modes/live-interview/live-interview-solve.command.ts
if (
  !extractedProblem.is_valid_problem ||
  !ALLOWED_PROBLEM_TYPES[AppMode.LIVE_INTERVIEW].includes(
    extractedProblem.problem_type,
  )
) {
  return {
    thoughts: [
      `The screenshot does not contain a supported problem type. ` +
      `Detected: ${extractedProblem.problem_type}`,
    ],
    // ...solve prompt is never called
  };
}

Only DSA and SQL make it through. A billing page comes back NOT_A_PROBLEM and is bounced before the expensive model ever runs. A system design question is recognized for what it is and turned away with a message that tells you why, instead of confidently faking an answer it has no business giving.

I want to be careful not to oversell this. I don’t have a metric for how often it fires, there’s no counter or analytics in the code measuring a rejection rate, so I’m not going to quote you a percentage I can’t back up. What I can tell you is what it does: it’s a cheap, deterministic filter that catches the dumbest and most common failure (wrong screenshot) before it costs anything, and it gives the model an honest way to say “that’s not something I solve” instead of hallucinating confidence.

3. Dark mode, light mode, and the thing I didn’t build

I expected theme to matter. Light text on a dark IDE versus dark text on a white page felt like the kind of thing that would trip up OCR and force me to write preprocessing, contrast normalization, maybe a grayscale pass.

I never wrote any of it. There is no theme detection, no contrast handling, no theme-aware preprocessing anywhere in the codebase. Every screenshot is treated identically. And in practice, modern vision models read both dark and light themes fine, so it simply hasn’t been a problem worth solving.

I’m including this not as a feature but as an honest non-event. The flip side of “I didn’t need to build it” is “there’s no safety net if it ever regresses.” If a future model update started struggling with low-contrast themes, nothing in the pipeline would catch it or compensate. It works today because the underlying model is good, not because Ezzi does anything clever.

4. Handwriting and whiteboard photos

This one is just a limitation, and I’d rather say so than dress it up.

The entire pipeline assumes a rendered screenshot, clean glyphs from an IDE or a coding platform, pixels generated by software. A phone photo of a whiteboard, or handwritten notes, is a completely different vision problem: variable lighting, perspective skew, handwriting, glare. The prompts don’t expect it and there’s no detection that would flag it.

Could the model sometimes read a tidy whiteboard? Maybe. But it isn’t designed for it, I haven’t tuned for it, and I wouldn’t trust it in the one moment that counts. If the problem is on a whiteboard, type it out and screenshot that. The tool is built for screens, and I’d rather be clear about the boundary than imply a capability I haven’t earned.

5. The debug loop: when the model has to actually look again

The solve stage throws the image away. The debug stage does the opposite, and it’s the one place where the expensive model reads pixels directly.

When you’ve got a solution and it’s failing tests, you screenshot the error and ask for a fix. That flow runs the error screenshot through a dedicated classifier that sorts what it’s looking at:

// src/solutions/types.ts
export enum IssueType {
  FAILING_TEST_CASES = 'FAILING_TEST_CASES',
  RUNTIME_ERROR = 'RUNTIME_ERROR',
  NOTHING_FOUND = 'NOTHING_FOUND',
}

A failing assertion is a different kind of problem from a stack trace, and NOTHING_FOUND exists precisely so the model can admit it doesn't see an actual error rather than inventing one. Then the debug prompt is told, plainly, what to do with it:

Consider errors provided in screenshot 3 and avoid writing code
that repeats those errors.

The reason debug can do this is that the whole conversation is rebuilt and replayed. Each solve-then-debug chain shares a conversation id, and prior steps are reconstructed into the message history so the model remembers the original problem and its own previous attempt:

// src/integrations/prompts/core/utils/prompt.utils.ts
buildConversationHistory(conversation: ConversationContext): MessageParam[] {
  const messages: MessageParam[] = [];
  for (const step of conversation.steps) {
    messages.push({ role: 'user', content: [{ type: 'text', text: step.request }] });
    messages.push({ role: 'assistant', content: [{ type: 'text', text: step.response }] });
  }
  return messages;
}

This is the engineered fix for “the model forgot what we were doing.” Without it, every debug would be a cold read of an error with no idea what problem it belonged to. With it, the model sees the arc: here was the problem, here’s what you wrote, here’s what broke, don’t do that again. Debug also runs at a higher effort budget with adaptive thinking turned on, because fixing a wrong answer is genuinely harder than producing the first one.

The Failure the Model Never Warns You About

Here’s the one that still bothers me, and it ties everything above together.

There is no confidence signal anywhere in this pipeline. The classification gate is binary, valid or not. When something throws, the user gets a generic “Error occurred.” What’s missing is any sense of doubt: the read stage can’t tell you it’s only 60% sure it parsed a constraint, and nothing flags a transcript that came off a low-quality image. The pipeline reports success and failure, but never uncertainty.

Stack that on top of the split-brain architecture and you get the genuinely dangerous case: Sonnet misreads a constraint, returns it at temperature zero with no hedging, Opus solves the misread version at high effort, and you receive a confident, well-commented, correctly-formatted solution to a problem that’s subtly not yours. Every layer did its job. The output looks exactly as trustworthy as a correct one.

A wrong answer that looks uncertain is easy to catch. A wrong answer that looks polished is not. If I were ranking what to build next, it wouldn’t be theme handling or whiteboard support. It would be a confidence signal, some way for the read stage to tell you when it isn’t sure, so you know to re-shoot before you trust the output. That’s the real gap, and I’d rather name it than hide it.

What I Learned

A few things that might transfer to anyone building on top of a vision model.

The failures get subtler as the models get better. A model that can’t read your screen at all is easy to deal with, you see garbage and try again. A model that reads it 98% right is harder, because the 2% is plausible and confident. Better vision moved my problem from “does it work” to “how do I know when it didn’t.”

Split the cheap reader from the expensive thinker, but respect the seam. Using Sonnet to read and classify before paying for an Opus solve is good engineering. It’s cheaper, faster, and it lets me gate junk early. But the seam between them is a string, and a string can’t carry uncertainty. The architecture that saves you money is the same one that hides the misread.

Most of the real mitigations are prompt-level and boring. The classification gate is a prompt and an if statement. The error-avoidance in debug is one sentence. The readable-names option is a string you append. There’s no computer vision wizardry in here. The leverage was in deciding what to ask the model and when to not call it at all.

Be honest about what you didn’t build. Theme handling, whiteboard support, a legibility check on compressed images, a confidence score, none of those exist. Some I skipped because the model made them unnecessary, one I skipped and shouldn’t have. Knowing which is which is the actual engineering.

The Bigger Picture

If you’re putting a vision model anywhere near the front of your product, the lesson isn’t “vision works now,” even though it mostly does. It’s that the interesting work starts after it works. Where does a confident misread go? What can’t catch it? What does the user see when the model is wrong but doesn’t know it?

For an interview assistant the stakes are small and the moment is yours to redo. For a medical scan, a legal document, a financial statement, the same architecture with the same blind seam is a much scarier thing. The pattern is identical: a cheap model reads, an expensive model reasons, and nothing in between admits doubt.

If you want to see exactly how this is wired, all of it is open source: github.com/GetEzzi/ezzi-app. The prompts, the gate, the capture layer, it’s all in there to read and pick apart.

If you’ve shipped a vision model into production, I’d like to hear how you handle the confident-but-wrong case. That’s the part nobody seems to have a clean answer for, and the war stories are where the real knowledge is.

I hope this was helpful. Good luck, and happy engineering!

title: Building a Local Multimodal Search Engine with Gemma 4 and Qdrant: A Step-by-Step Build Guide
partialText:
How I made hours of video, audio, and text searchable by plain language, and how you can rebuild it from scratch, entirely on your own machine

What we’re building (and why)

That single constraint, local first, shaped every decision in this build. It is the reason the architecture looks the way it does, and it’s also why this is a tutorial about two tools doing a lot of work locally: Gemma 4 (served by Ollama) for understanding pixels and audio, and Qdrant for storing and searching vectors.

This guide walks the whole thing from an empty folder to a working search engine, in the order I actually built it:

  1. Set up the environment (uv, FFmpeg, Ollama, models)
  2. Understand the one design decision that makes multimodal search work: describe-then-embed
  3. Install and choose Qdrant, and why I picked it
  4. Design the Qdrant schema for moments, not files (the heart of this tutorial)
  5. Build the describe-then-embed bridge with Gemma 4
  6. Build the ingestion pipeline (how to actually get data in)
  7. Query: per-space search, fusion, MaxSim, rerank
  8. Route the questions retrieval shouldn’t answer (counting, inventory)
  9. Stream the answers, add guardrails, and learn from the performance traps

Let’s go.

Step 0: Prerequisites and environment

You need three things on the machine before running Python:

  1. macOS (Apple Silicon recommended) or Linux
  2. `uv`, the Python package/venv manager this project uses
  3. `ffmpeg`, every video/audio extraction step shells out to it

Two models, two jobs:

  • `gemma4:e4b`, the multimodal brain. It reads images and listens to audio natively, and it also drives query-intent analysis, reranking, and the RAG chat. The E in E4B stands for effective parameters: an efficient design that keeps the memory footprint friendly on Apple Silicon while keeping vision and audio in the same model.
  • `nomic-embed-text`, a dedicated text embedder that maps everything into one unified 768-dimensional space.
Don’t have the weights yet? The whole pipeline, ingest, index, search, RAG runs against a deterministic hash-based stub so you can develop offline and in CI:
DEEPSEARCH_USE_STUB=true uv run uvicorn deepsearch.api.main:app — port 8000 ``

The “two-model trap” I avoided

The obvious first instinct is to reach for a pipeline with three or four specialist models: one for speech-to-text, one for OCR on the frames, one vision-language model for the screen, and glue to stitch the outputs together. That works, and it’s a maintenance tax you pay forever. Four downloads, four sets of version drift, four failure modes.

Gemma 4 changed that: one model reads images and listens to audio. So the model question was settled early, and the interesting problem moved to retrieval, which is where Qdrant comes in.

Step 1: The one idea that makes multimodal search work: describe, then embed

Before any schema, you have to internalise the single most important design decision in the system. Get this wrong and nothing downstream matters.

Here is the trap, and it’s a good one because it sounds correct:

“Gemma is multimodal, so I’ll embed the video frames into vectors, embed the audio into vectors, embed the text into vectors, store all of them in Qdrant, and at query time embed the user’s question and search across all three spaces. Cross-modal search, solved.”

It does not work. Gemma 4 is a generative decoder. It is not a contrastive dual-encoder like CLIP or ImageBind. Models like CLIP are trained with one specific objective: to push an image and its caption close together in a shared space. Gemma has no such objective. Its internal image activations are optimised for predicting the next token, not for sitting near the text that describes them.

If you index raw frame activations and search them with a text query vector, you’re comparing two things in different coordinate systems. The cosine similarity is close to noise. You’ll get results, and they’ll be confidently wrong.

The fix: stop treating Gemma as an embedder and start treating it as a translator.

  1. Gemma describes each keyframe in a sentence or two.
  2. Gemma (or Whisper, more on that later) transcribes each audio chunk into text.
  3. Captions are already text.

Now every modality is text, and a single dedicated embedder (nomic-embed-text) maps all of it into one unified 768-dimensional space. The user query gets embedded by the same model into the same space. A natural-language query now genuinely retrieves across video, audio, and text, because everything, including the question, lives in one coordinate system.

Step 2: Installing Qdrant (and why I chose it)

Why Qdrant

I evaluated several vector databases for this architecture, and Qdrant emerged as the optimal choice due to its alignment with local-first, multimodal constraints:

Qdrant Documentation Link: https://qdrant.tech/documentation/

  1. Embedded, Zero-Infrastructure Deployment: The primary constraint is a local-first environment without cloud dependencies. Qdrant’s Python client provides an in-process, disk-backed database — QdrantClient(path=”./qdrant_storage”) — that requires no Docker or daemons. This turns the project into a portable laptop tool.
  2. Seamless Scalability: The application code is agnostic to the database topology. By toggling the DEEPSEARCH_QDRANT_URL environment variable, the same codebase transitions from embedded local storage to a remote Qdrant server, enabling fleet-wide scaling without rewriting the storage logic.
  3. First-Class Named Vectors: Qdrant supports multiple independently searchable vector fields per point. This maps perfectly to our requirement to manage distinct text, video, and audio embedding spaces within a single collection, eliminating the need to synchronise separate indexes.
  4. Native ColBERT-style MaxSim: Late-interaction retrieval is a native concept rather than an implementation challenge, providing efficient multi-vector support out of the box.
  5. Integrated Quantisation and Filtering: Features like INT8 scalar quantisation (to optimise index size in unified memory) and metadata pre-filtering are simple configurations rather than engineering hurdles.

These are simple configurations, not heavy engineering tasks.

Option A — Embedded local mode (the default, recommended to start)

There is nothing to install beyond the Python client, which uv pip install -e. already pulled (qdrant-client>=1.12). The store simply opens a folder:

# src/deepsearch/vectorstore/store.py
def _connect(self) -> QdrantClient:
    url = self.settings.qdrant.url.strip()
    if url:                                   # server mode
        log.info(f"Connecting to Qdrant server at {url}")
        return QdrantClient(url=url)
    path = self.settings.qdrant_storage_path  # embedded local mode
    path.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    log.info(f"Using embedded Qdrant (local mode) at {path}")
    return QdrantClient(path=str(path))

With DEEPSEARCH_QDRANT_URL empty (the default), the index lives in ./qdrant_storage. Done. No server.

Option B — Qdrant as a server (when you want the dashboard or scale)

When you outgrow embedded mode, you want the web dashboard, or you want several processes hitting one index, flip to a server with Docker:

docker compose up -d                       # starts qdrant on :6333 (REST) / :6334 (gRPC)
export DEEPSEARCH_QDRANT_URL=http://localhost:6333

The docker-compose.yml is tiny:

services:
  qdrant:
    image: qdrant/qdrant:latest
    container_name: deepsearch-qdrant
    ports:
      - "6333:6333"   # REST / dashboard at http://localhost:6333/dashboard
      - "6334:6334"   # gRPC
    volumes:
      - ./qdrant_storage:/qdrant/storage
    restart: unless-stopped

Step 3: Designing the Qdrant schema for moments, not files

This is the heart of the build. Two requirements pull against each other here, and how you resolve the tension determines whether timestamps are free or impossible.

Requirement 1: Multivectors (ColBERT-style late interaction)

Qdrant supports an array of vectors per named field, scored with MaxSim, the ColBERT-style late-interaction idea. A single asset (a whole video) can hold, say twenty keyframe vectors, and you score the entire asset by its best-matching frame. This gives fast, high-recall asset-level retrieval: “Which files are even relevant?”

Requirement 2: Accurate playback

You don’t want to know that a file matches. You want the exact offset so the player can seek to the second.

Why they fight

Asset-level MaxSim gives you one score per asset and throws away the sub-vector matched. You lose the timestamp. So you cannot make the multivector point your primary retrieval unit, not if pinpoint playback is the whole point.

The resolution: the fragment is the primary retrieval unit

So I index at two granularities in one collection:

  1. Fragment points (primary). One Qdrant point per keyframe, per audio chunk, per caption line. Each fragment populates exactly one of three named single-vector spaces and carries a payload with the precise offsets. These are what make timestamps free.
  2. Asset-level MaxSim points (secondary). One point per asset holding the array of that asset’s frame/audio vectors, in two multivector spaces, for fast recall.

The three named single-vector spaces and the two multivector spaces:

# src/deepsearch/vectorstore/schema.py
# Fragment-level, temporal targeting, one populated per fragment point.
NAMED_VECTORS = ("text_descriptions", "video_frames", "audio_chunks")
 
# Asset-level MaxSim multivector spaces (ColBERT-style arrays per asset).
MULTIVECTOR_VECTORS = ("frames_maxsim", "audio_maxsim")

And the fragment data model — note that the payload carries start_s / end_s, which is where second-accurate playback comes from:

@dataclass
class Fragment:
    asset_id: str               # stable id shared by all fragments of one file
    asset_name: str
    file_path: str              # absolute path to the source media on disk
    modality: Modality          # TEXT | VIDEO | AUDIO
    text: str                   # description / transcript / caption (this is what gets embedded)
    start_s: float = 0.0        # fragment start offset within the asset
    end_s: float = 0.0          # fragment end offset within the asset
    duration_s: float = 0.0
    category: str = "uncategorized"
    thumbnail_path: str | None = None
    ingested_at: int = ...
    point_id: str = ...
 
# Payload fields indexed for fast pre-filtering:
KEYWORD_INDEXES = ("asset_id", "modality", "category")
INTEGER_INDEXES = ("ingested_at",)

Creating the collection (the multivector setup, line by line)

Here is ensure_collection, the one function that declares the whole schema:

# src/deepsearch/vectorstore/store.py
def ensure_collection(self, recreate: bool = False) -> None:
    dim = self._embedding_dim()      # 768 for nomic-embed-text (probed live at startup)
    distance = self._distance()      # Cosine
 
    # 1) Three single-vector named spaces  , one per modality (fragment level).
    vectors = {
        name: models.VectorParams(size=dim, distance=distance)
        for name in NAMED_VECTORS    # text_descriptions, video_frames, audio_chunks
    }
 
    # 2) Two MaxSim multivector spaces (ColBERT-style late interaction, asset level).
    for name in MULTIVECTOR_VECTORS:  # frames_maxsim, audio_maxsim
        vectors[name] = models.VectorParams(
            size=dim,
            distance=distance,
            multivector_config=models.MultiVectorConfig(
                comparator=models.MultiVectorComparator.MAX_SIM
            ),
        )
 
    # 3) Create the collection with INT8 scalar quantization (always in RAM).
    self.client.create_collection(
        collection_name=self.collection,
        vectors_config=vectors,
        quantization_config=self._quantization(),   # scalar INT8, always_ram
    )
 
    # 4) Payload indexes so Qdrant can PRE-FILTER before the vector search.
    for field in KEYWORD_INDEXES:    # asset_id, modality, category
        self.client.create_payload_index(
            self.collection, field, models.PayloadSchemaType.KEYWORD
        )
    for field in INTEGER_INDEXES:    # ingested_at
        self.client.create_payload_index(
            self.collection, field, models.PayloadSchemaType.INTEGER
        )

Four things are happening, and each earns its place:

  1. Named single-vector spaces: the fragment-level spaces a text query searches directly.
  2. MaxSim multivector spaces: declared with MultiVectorConfig(comparator=MAX_SIM). This is the entire multivector setup — same dimension, same distance, plus the MaxSim comparator. That one line is what turns a named field into a ColBERT-style array.
  3. Scalar quantisation: compresses the vectors to INT8 and pins them in RAM (always_ram). This is what lets the database coexist with a multi-gigabyte model inside the same unified memory on a laptop.
  4. Payload indexes: they let Qdrant pre-filter before the vector search runs, so a query like “only videos added in the last thirty days” becomes a cheap keyword + integer filter instead of a full scan.

Writing a fragment point

Each fragment populates exactly one named vector, the one matching its modality:

def upsert_fragments(self, fragments, vectors) -> int:
    points = []
    for frag, vec in zip(fragments, vectors, strict=True):
        points.append(
            models.PointStruct(
                id=frag.point_id,
                vector={frag.modality.value: vec},  # populate ONE named space
                payload=frag.payload(),             # asset_id, file_path, start_s, end_s, …
            )
        )
    if points:
        self.client.upsert(self.collection, points=points, wait=True)
    return len(points)

Writing the asset-level MaxSim point

One point per asset, holding the arrays of frame and audio vectors. The point ID is namespaced so it never collides with a fragment ID:

def upsert_asset_multivectors(self, asset_id, payload, frame_vectors, audio_vectors):
    vec: dict[str, list[list[float]]] = {}
    if frame_vectors:
        vec["frames_maxsim"] = frame_vectors   # array of N frame vectors
    if audio_vectors:
        vec["audio_maxsim"] = audio_vectors    # array of M audio vectors
    if not vec:
        return
    point_id = str(uuid.uuid5(uuid.NAMESPACE_OID, f"asset:{asset_id}"))
    self.client.upsert(
        self.collection,
        points=[models.PointStruct(id=point_id, vector=vec, payload=payload)],
        wait=True,
    )

A sharp edge worth flagging: compute MaxSim client-side in embedded mode

Here’s a gotcha that cost me time. The embedded Qdrant client (the on-disk, no-server mode) does not reliably run native multivector queries. I tried both the 1-D and 2-D query shapes and got internal errors. The portable fix is to compute MaxSim on the client: scroll the asset-level points, take the maximum dot product between the query vector and each stored sub-vector, and rank. Because all vectors are L2-normalised, the dot product is cosine similarity. This runs identically in embedded and server mode:

def search_maxsim(self, vector_name, query_vector, limit, query_filter=None):
    records, _ = self.client.scroll(
        self.collection, scroll_filter=query_filter,
        limit=10_000, with_payload=True, with_vectors=[vector_name],
    )
    scored = []
    for r in records:
        vecs = (r.vector or {}).get(vector_name) if isinstance(r.vector, dict) else None
        if not vecs:
            continue
        best = max(_dot(query_vector, sub) for sub in vecs)   # MaxSim
        scored.append(models.ScoredPoint(id=r.id, version=0, score=best, payload=r.payload))
    scored.sort(key=lambda p: p.score, reverse=True)
    return scored[:limit]
The takeaway for this section: pick your retrieval unit before anything else. Fragments-versus-assets is not a detail; it decides whether timestamps are free or impossible. I get both: fragments for the exact second, an asset-level MaxSim point for fast recall, all in one Qdrant collection.

Step 4: The describe-then-embed bridge (Gemma 4 client)

Now make Step 1 real. The model client never pretends to produce retrieval embeddings from pixels; it produces words, which the embedder then turns into vectors.

# src/deepsearch/models/gemma.py
def describe_image(self, image_path) -> str:
    if self.is_stub:
        return f"[stub frame description for {Path(image_path).name}]"
    b64 = _b64_file(image_path)
    resp = self._invoke(
        self._client.generate,
        model=self.settings.models.gemma_model,
        prompt=_FRAME_PROMPT,
        images=[b64],
        options=self._desc_opts(),
        keep_alive=self.settings.models.keep_alive,
        think=False,        # see note below
    )
    return resp["response"].strip()

Two details earn their place:

  1. `think=False`. Gemma 4 is a thinking model. If you let it think while capping the output budget (num_predict), the reasoning tokens eat the budget, and you get an empty answer. I learned that the hard way: ingestion produced zero fragments and crashed on an empty vector. Turning thinking off for description/transcription fixed it.
  2. `keep_alive` (30m). Keeps the weights resident in VRAM between calls so the next one doesn’t reload the model, a big latency win on local Apple Silicon.

The embedding side is just as plain, empty input is guarded, and the dimension is checked, so a misconfigured model fails instead of silently corrupting the index:

def embed_text(self, texts: list[str]) -> list[list[float]]:
    if not texts:
        return []
    out = []
    ka = self.settings.models.keep_alive
    for text in texts:
        prompt = text if text and text.strip() else " "   # never send an empty prompt
        resp = self._invoke(self._client.embeddings,
                            model=self.embed_model_name, prompt=prompt, keep_alive=ka)
        vec = list(resp.get("embedding") or [])
        if len(vec) != self.dim:
            raise ValueError(f"Embedding model returned {len(vec)} dims (expected {self.dim}).")
        out.append(_normalize(vec))   # L2-normalise so dot product == cosine
    return out

Note the _normalise at the end, that’s the invariant the client-side MaxSim relies on.

Step 5: The ingestion pipeline (how to actually ingest)

With the schema and the bridge in place, ingestion is the orchestration that fills the index. For each file:

video  → keyframes (described) + audio chunks (transcribed) + sidecar captions
audio  → audio chunks (transcribed)
image  → single description
text   → timed/untimed segments

Run it

From the CLI:

# Index a single file or a whole folder
uv run deepsearch ingest ./data/media --category meetings
 
# Or via the Make target
make ingest P=./data/media C=meetings

Or from the UI: open the Ingest tab, drop in video/audio/.srt/.vtt/text, pick a category, click Ingest. The backend streams live progress over Server-Sent Events.

What happens inside ingest_file

self.store.ensure_collection()      # create the schema if needed (idempotent)
asset_id = _asset_id(path)          # stable sha1 of the resolved path
self.store.delete_asset(asset_id)   # re-ingest REPLACES, never duplicates
# ... build fragments per modality ...
fragments = [f for f in fragments if (f.text or "").strip()]  # drop empties (zero-vectors break upsert)
self._embed_and_upsert(fragments, progress)

Keyframes come from scene-boundary detection (PySceneDetect’s content detector), falling back to uniform sampling, capped at max_keyframes (12 by default, fewer Gemma vision calls = much faster ingest). Each keyframe is written as a JPEG (used both as the Gemma input and the UI thumbnail) and tagged with its timestamp.

Audio is normalised to 16 kHz mono WAV via FFmpeg (with optional afftdn denoise), then transcribed — see the performance note below for which transcriber.

Embedding and the dual write happen together in _embed_and_upsert: fragments are embedded in batches, each batch is upserted as fragment points, and the per-modality vectors are accumulated so that, at the end, a single asset-level MaxSim point is written:

def _embed_and_upsert(self, fragments, progress):
    frame_vecs, audio_vecs, asset_payload = [], [], None
    for group in _batched(fragments, self.settings.ingestion.batch_size):
        vectors = self.model.embed_text([f.text for f in group])
        self.store.upsert_fragments(group, vectors)          # fragment points
        for frag, vec in zip(group, vectors, strict=True):
            asset_payload = asset_payload or {... "kind": "asset"}
            if frag.modality is Modality.VIDEO:   frame_vecs.append(vec)
            elif frag.modality is Modality.AUDIO: audio_vecs.append(vec)
    if asset_payload and (frame_vecs or audio_vecs):
        self.store.upsert_asset_multivectors(           # ONE asset-level MaxSim point
            asset_payload["asset_id"], asset_payload, frame_vecs, audio_vecs
        )

Verify it landed

uv run deepsearch stats
# assets=1 fragments=37 by_modality={'video_frames': 12, 'audio_chunks': 24, 'text_descriptions': 1}

Step 6: Querying: per-space search, fusion, MaxSim, rerank

A search runs: safety filter → intent → embed → per-space prefetch → fuse → (optional) rerank → timestamped hits.

# src/deepsearch/query/search.py
qvec = self.model.embed_query(query)
flt = build_filter(categories, modalities, ingested_after)   # payload pre-filter
 
# Only query spaces with non-trivial weight (saves work for focused intents).
spaces = [s for s in NAMED_VECTORS if weights.get(s, 0.0) > 0.01] or list(NAMED_VECTORS)
per_space = {
    space: self.store.search_named(space, qvec, cfg.prefetch_limit, flt)
    for space in spaces
}
 
strategy = "weighted" if weights_override is not None else cfg.fusion
fused = fusion_mod.fuse(per_space, strategy, weights)
 
top = fused[: cfg.rerank_top_n] if cfg.rerank else fused[: cfg.top_k]
if cfg.rerank and len(top) > 1:
    top = rerank(query, top, cfg.rerank_top_n)
hits = [self._to_hit(h) for h in top][: cfg.top_k]

Fusion is a client-side decision, not a Qdrant feature

A lot of write-ups imply you can hand Qdrant a weight per named vector and let it blend the spaces. You can’t. Qdrant fuses candidate lists you define (via its Query API, prefetch, and RRF/DBSF); the weighting across named spaces happens in your code. So the engine searches each weighted space, then fuses:

  1. RRF (Reciprocal Rank Fusion) is the default, rank-based and scale-free, so it doesn’t care that the three spaces produce scores on different scales.
  2. Weighted kicks in when the user drags the weight sliders. That was a real bug at first: the weights existed, but the default RRF ignored them, so the sliders did nothing until the engine learned to honour an explicit override (strategy = “weighted” if weights_override is None).

One honest tradeoff: rerank is slow

The Gemma rerank is a listwise prompt, and on a local 4-billion-effective-parameter model, a single rerank call can run for tens of seconds. So rerank and the LLM intent step are off by default for fast local search; you flip them on per request when quality matters more than latency. RRF on its own is already strong.

Step 7: Route the questions retrieval shouldn’t answer

Some questions are not retrieval questions, and knowing which to route away from the model is half of making a grounded assistant feel trustworthy.

Counting. “How many times is finance mentioned?” must never be a model guess; it will round, hedge, and miss occurrences outside the top results. So counting is deterministic: scan every fragment, count exact substring matches, and report the number with timestamps. No model in the loop.

def _count(self, term: str) -> dict:
    needle = term.lower()
    total, sources, per_asset = 0, [], {}
    for p in self.store.all_fragments():
        n = (p.get("text") or "").lower().count(needle)
        if n:
            total += n
            per_asset[p["asset_name"]] = per_asset.get(p["asset_name"], 0) + n
            sources.append(Source(...))
    # ... report total + timestamps ...

Inventory. “What types of files do I have?” is answered straight from the asset list, counted once per asset, with no sources, because no single fragment answers a library-wide question.

Step 8: Stream the answer, then lock it down

Streaming, because waiting in silence feels broken

The interface is a chat: FastAPI backend, Next.js frontend, answer streamed token-by-token. A chat that freezes for forty seconds and dumps a wall of text feels broken even when it’s working; a chat that types feels alive. Retrieval and deterministic routing happen first, then the LLM tokens flow as Server-Sent Events, then a final event carries the sources:

@app.post("/api/ask/stream")
def ask_stream(req: schemas.AskRequest) -> StreamingResponse:
    _require_live_backend()
    history = [{"role": m.role, "content": m.content} for m in req.history]
 
    def sse():
        for kind, data in get_rag().stream(req.question, history):
            if kind == "token":
                yield f"data: {json.dumps({'type': 'token', 'data': data})}\n\n"
            else:
                yield f"data: {json.dumps({'type': 'sources', 'data': serialize(data)})}\n\n"
 
    return StreamingResponse(sse(), media_type="text/event-stream",
                             headers={"Cache-Control": "no-cache", "X-Accel-Buffering": "no"})

One subtle production note. The Next.js dev proxy must point at 127.0.0.1, not localhost. Node resolves localhost to IPv6 first, the Python server binds IPv4 only, and your logs fill with connection refused, while the browser looks fine.

Guardrails: the system would be unsafe without them

Three guardrails earn their keep:

  1. A prompt-injection pre-filter runs on the query before any vector lookup, so a query trying to hijack the instructions never reaches the model.
  2. A description sanitiser scrubs what Gemma generates, because a video can contain adversarial on-screen text that the model would otherwise transcribe and later obey.
  3. An ingest semaphore serialises heavy jobs, so uploading three long videos queues them instead of thrashing the GPU.

Step 9: The long-video problem, and what actually fixed it

A fifty-seven-minute lecture took more than ten minutes to index. Unacceptable, and the profiler told a clear story in ten seconds. Keyframes were capped at twelve, so vision was cheap. Audio was the killer: thirty-second chunks over fifty-seven minutes is ~137 chunks, each a separate Gemma audio call, run one after another.

Two changes fixed it:

  1. Concurrency. Describe/transcribe calls now run through a thread pool; Ollama serves parallel requests for roughly 3× throughput.
  2. A dedicated speech model. Audio transcription has moved to faster-whisper, which transcribes in a single fast pass rather than one model call per chunk. In a real lecture, it ran at ~14× real time, so 57 minutes of audio finished in a few minutes. Because Whisper runs on the CPU, it overlaps with Gemma vision on the GPU.

The purity of “Gemma does everything” bent a little here, and that’s fine: a dedicated speech model is the right tool for an hour of audio. The Gemma audio path stays available behind a config flag (audio_backend: gemma) for anyone who wants it.

What I’d tell another engineer before they start

  • Pick your retrieval unit before anything else. Fragments versus assets is not a detail; it decides whether timestamps are free or impossible. In Qdrant, I got both in one collection.
  • Don’t assume a generative model gives you a metric space. It doesn’t. Describe, then embed the bridge.
  • Route the questions that have exact answers away from the LLM. Counting and inventory belong to plain code.
  • Measure before you optimize. I was certain the bottleneck was scene detection. It was audio, and the profiler said so in ten seconds.
  • Let your storage layer be the easy part. Qdrant’s embedded-to-server continuum, named vectors, native MaxSim, payload filtering, and quantisation meant the database was the one thing I never had to fight. Choose tools that let you keep your attention on the hard problem.

The whole thing runs on a laptop, indexes an hour of footage in a few minutes, answers in plain language, and lands you on the exact second. No cloud, no keys, no data leaving the machine. That was the entire point.

Clone it, point it at your own messy folder, and ask it something only you can ask.

The series I planned called this part “The plan is stale the moment you ship it.” Then I sat down to write it, and the plan was stale.

One of the lessons I’d planned to write up — a small pattern for piping transient state through a domain aggregate — didn’t fit the shape of an article. The plan-going-stale lesson alone wouldn’t carry one. The four lessons that did hang together share a different thread, and it isn’t “plans go stale.” Plans going stale is just one of them.

What they share is this: the plan went stale in the spots where it tried to hold the current state. Four day-one decisions outlived it because they live somewhere the code can’t silently drift away from.

This article is the thing it describes. Here’s what stayed.

The plan, and the part of it that didn’t rot

Before a single C# file existed, the project had a 1,200-line docs/plan.md covering the solution layout, the project-reference rules, the database schema, and the phased build order. It was the document that paid back the hardest. Every time I asked, "Where does this live?" the answer was on the page. Every time I asked "what's next," I already had a phase to point at.

It also went stale.

The lobby section is in plan.md describes a flow that no longer exists. GameLobby.razor was rebuilt twice as I learned what joining a game actually feels like for a tester, and the plan wasn’t updated either time. By the time I noticed, the doc was lying — confidently — about a feature shipped three months earlier. I deleted the section because rewriting it would have meant rewriting it again next month.

Other parts of the same document are still load-bearing. The project-reference rule — Web and Mobile may not reference Api, Services, or Infrastructure; they talk over HTTP and SignalR only — is on the page in the plan, in CLAUDE.md, and enforced by the .csproj graph. It hasn't moved. Three feature reorganizations didn't touch it, because the rule lives somewhere the features can't reach.

That’s the difference, and it’s what this article is about. The lobby section tried to hold both the decision (“here’s how lobby works”) and the current state (“here’s what GameLobby.razor does today"). The current state always wins. The state drifted with the code, and the section underneath rotted silently. The project-reference rule only ever held the decision (there is no "current state" of may not reference, there's just the rule), so there was nothing for the code to drift away from.

The plan was useful for exactly the parts where the decision was the whole content. The plan was the receipt for those decisions. The decisions outlived the plan because they sat on shelves the code couldn’t reach — and the rest of this article is about three of those shelves, plus the counterexample I’m paying for in real time.

The layers — and the two shelves the rules sit on

The UpAllNight solution is split into seven projects: Api, Services, Infrastructure, Contracts, App, Web, and Mobile, plus a separate SSDT Database project. A new feature touches six of them — a stored procedure, a repository, a service, a controller, a contract DTO, and an SDK client call. The temptation to skip the layers and write Controller -> Dapper directly was, and still is, real.

I didn’t. The layers paid back in two specific ways.

The Blazor App project is shared by both Web (Blazor WebAssembly host) and Mobile (.NET MAUI Blazor Hybrid). Pages live in App; the hosts are thin shells. Mobile shipped without a parallel UI codebase, and it stayed that way through the rebuilds, because Web couldn't touch mobile-specific concerns and Mobile couldn't touch browser-specific ones.

The Contracts assembly is the only thing both clients and the server reference. Changing a request shape produces compile errors at every consumer — browser, mobile, SDK — at build time. Not at runtime, not in a Postman test, at build time. That's the rule earning its keep, every PR.

What kept those rules from drifting was that they didn’t live in the C# files. They lived in two places the C# files can’t reach.

CLAUDE.md holds the why. "Web and Mobile may not reference Api, Services, or Infrastructure — they communicate over HTTP and SignalR only." That sentence is one line. It's been one line for a year. No PR has touched it. The C# can rearrange itself however a feature needs it to, and the line sits there unmoved.

The .csproj graph holds the what. The Web.csproj doesn't list Api.csproj as a project reference. If a contributor types using UpAllNight.Api.Whatever; inside Web, they get a build error before they get a code review. The rule is mechanical. The .csproj files are the enforcement; CLAUDE.md is the explanation.

The combination is what held. Either alone wouldn’t have. A documented rule without the build graph is aspirational: easy to forget, easy to violate quietly. A build graph without the documented rule is mysterious — the next contributor adds a reference, the compiler complains, they don’t know why, so they restructure the wrong thing to make the error go away.

The layer rules outlived three feature reorganizations because they were pinned to two shelves the features didn’t get to touch.

Memory, or: corrections that stop costing twice

The third shelf is project-level memory in Claude Code. The corrections I’ve made once become memories the next session opens with.

Two have paid back across more sessions than I can count.

The first is a feedback memory captured after the seed-script incident from Part 1: seed scripts must be idempotent — guard with IF NOT EXISTS per row or per block; never raw INSERT. Every subsequent generated-asset seed file inherits it without me asking. The avatar generator, the deck generator, the lobby background generator — none have produced a seed script that failed on second deploy. Not because I told them to, but because the rule loads before the work starts.

The second is a project memory documenting an intentional deferred decision: book-strip symmetry follow-up — container-relative sizing is deliberately deferred, here’s why. That note exists because I caught myself, three sessions in a row, re-litigating the same “shouldn’t the book strips be proportional?” conversation. The memory is short. It says: yes, eventually; no, not yet; here’s the reason. The next session opens with the decision settled. Three sessions of re-arguing collapsed to zero.

The pattern is small and load-bearing: every correction goes into memory before it goes back into the code. When I notice myself fixing the same thing twice, the third occurrence isn’t fixing the code first; it’s writing the rule into memory and then fixing the code. Otherwise the next session has nothing to anchor on, and the correction has to be re-derived by whoever shows up.

This is the same shape as the layer rules. The memory lives somewhere the code can’t reach. The code keeps iterating; the rule keeps loading. The two don’t drift apart because the code never had a way to touch the rule.

Provisioning, or: the lesson I’m living in real time

The fourth lesson is the one I’m paying the cost of right now. It’s a proof by counterexample.

The payment seam from Part 3 — the IPaymentProvider interface, the Stripe + Apple + Google wiring, the idempotent grant keyed on (Provider, ProviderTransactionId) — is built. The unit tests pass. The MAUI host picks the right native provider via conditional compilation. The webhook controller handles the Stripe shape and the receipt-validation controller handles the Apple/Google shape. The seam works.

None of it has run a real sandbox purchase end-to-end.

It can’t, because three external accounts the code depends on don’t exist yet. The Apple Developer account isn’t approved. The Mac required for the Apple build (MacInCloud, in my case) isn’t provisioned. The Play Console account is in review. The Google Cloud Pub/Sub topic Play Billing needs for server notifications isn’t created. Every one of those is a multi-day process, and some of them are serial: the Pub/Sub topic can’t be created until the Play Console is approved. I am writing this with the entire economy stack built and unit-tested, and zero ability to prove any of it works in front of a real store.

The provisioning lesson is a sentence in plan.md. That's exactly the problem. A sentence in the plan is not a date on a calendar. A sentence goes stale when the feature it gates gets reshuffled. A date on a calendar — or better, a multi-week task on whatever you actually look at every Monday — does not. Calendars don't drift to fit the code.

The retroactive rule: paid external accounts with multi-day approvals belong on the critical path, not in the doc. Day-one ask on the next project, in writing, before any code that depends on the answer: what paid external thing does this feature need, and what is its approval clock? That answer goes on a calendar. The plan can describe it, but the calendar is what makes it survive.

I am writing this section because I am paying the cost of not having written it earlier.

What outlives the plan

Four lessons, one shelf each. Project-reference rules on CLAUDE.md and the .csproj graph. Past corrections in project memory. External-account approvals on the calendar. None of them live in the C# files, and that is exactly why they outlived the plan. The C# iterated. The shelves didn't.

What didn’t outlive the plan was every section that tried to be both the rule and the current state. The lobby notes. The provisioning sentence. The transient-flag pattern I cut from this article — I’d told myself it would still feel sharp in Part 4, and it had already gone stale by the time I sat down to type it.

The plan is the receipt. The rules outlive it because they live where the code can’t reach.

This was supposed to be the article about plans going stale. It still is. It just has a different name on it.
